title: Renormalization for Robust Memory without Synchronization
abstract: Local error correction can preserve classical information against noise, but protection under synchronized updates need not survive when sites evolve at independent random times. Establishing stability is particularly challenging when protection relies on the collective action of competing local rules. Here we develop a spacetime renormalization framework that reveals how independently acting local updates can collectively stabilize memory. We identify sufficient conditions under which the geometry of stable interfaces and suppression of defect propagation produce reliable erosion at large scales. Applying this framework, we prove stability of the asynchronous \textsf{R} squeezing code and introduce robust processes in two and three dimensions. In these systems, both encoded phases persist under sufficiently weak noise, even when the noise favors one phase. Our results provide a criterion for designing autonomous memories sustained by competing local stochastic dynamics.
summary: This work introduces a spacetime renormalization framework to analyze memory retention in local systems operating under asynchronous, noisy dynamics. By comparing coarse-grained evolution paths, the authors establish rigorous stability criteria for codes like the R squeezing code. This provides a powerful tool for designing autonomous memory elements sustained by competing local stochastic processes.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of establishing robust memory in local update systems when the dynamics are subject to random local errors and asynchronous updates, where synchronization assumptions fail.
main_result: The authors develop a spacetime renormalization framework to prove stability for the asynchronous R squeezing code and introduce robust processes in 2D and 3D, showing memory persistence even when noise favors one phase.
method: The core method is a spacetime renormalization framework that compares coarse-grained evolution paths, allowing the derivation of stability criteria for continuous-time Markov processes.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a cellular automaton on a lattice undergoing continuous-time, asynchronous updates governed by local stochastic rules (e.g., the R squeezing code).
key_observables: Erosion property, relaxation gap, defect droplet size, and the probability of defect survival.
important_parameters: Noise strength ($\epsilon$), system dimension ($d=2, 3$), and the coarse-graining scale ($H$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on showing that the deviation between synchronous and asynchronous evolution paths is suppressed in the large-scale limit.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the difference between synchronous and asynchronous updates, and the spacetime renormalization argument comparing two evolution paths.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the problem of asynchronous stability to developing the renormalization framework, applying it to prove stability for specific codes, and finally analyzing the dimensional dependence of stability (2D vs 3D R process).
why_interesting: The techniques developed for analyzing memory in asynchronous stochastic dynamics are highly relevant to open quantum systems, particularly those modeled by local Hamiltonians or Lindblad master equations where noise and non-Markovian effects are present.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Synchronous and asynchronous updates. (a) Under synchronous updates, all sites are updated simultane- ously at each discrete time step. (b) Under asynchronous updates on a system of N sites, each time step is divided into N substeps, and one randomly chosen site is updated at each substep. Thus, each site is updated once on average per time step, although the order and number of updates at individual sites are random. As N →∞, with substep duration 1/N, the update clocks on any fixed finite collection of sites con- verge to independent rate-one Poisson processes.
